content: The University of Aberdeen School of Medicine, part of the College of Life Sciences and Medicine at the University of Aberdeen, has a long-standing history dating back to the founding of King’s College in 1495. It is recognized as the first English-speaking medical school in the world. Locations Currently, the medical school operates primarily from the Foresterhill site in Aberdeen. However, undergraduate teaching, particularly in anatomy, also takes place at Marischal College. The primary teaching hospitals include Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, Aberdeen Maternity Hospital, the Royal Aberdeen Children’s Hospital, Woodend Hospital, and the Royal Cornhill Hospital. Additionally, teaching is conducted in Inverness, mainly at Raigmore Hospital, and in Elgin at Dr. Gray’s Hospital, as well as at various other hospitals across the Highlands and Islands. People The current Dean of the School is Professor Michael Greaves, a Consultant Haematologist. The school also has two active Regius Professorships: the Regius Chair of Medicine and the Regius Chair of Surgery. The Regius Chairs of Midwifery and Anatomy are currently in abeyance. Education The school offers three undergraduate degree programs: Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MB ChB) Bachelor of Science in Medical Science (BSc Hons) Bachelor of Science in Health Science (BSc Hons) Postgraduate degrees are available as taught courses, typically leading to a Master of Science (MSc), or as research degrees at the master’s (MSc, MRes, ChM) or doctoral (PhD, MD) levels. MB ChB Course Structure The MB ChB program spans five years and is divided into four phases: Phase I (Year 1): Fundamentals of Medical Sciences Students begin with a short course on Basic Science in Medicine, including lectures in physiology and biochemistry. This is followed by system-based lectures and anatomy sessions addressing normal aspects of each system, complemented by practical sessions. A weekly Community Course introduces students to healthcare services in the community, such as visiting families with newborns. Communication skills are developed through small group tutorials and role-play in the Clinical Skills Centre. A four-week Student Selected Component allows students to explore healthcare topics in depth, conduct research, and present their findings. Phase II (Year 2 and two-thirds of Year 3): Principles of Clinical Medicine This phase starts with an introductory course on the Principles of Disease, followed by system-based lectures focusing on diseases and their abnormal aspects. The Community Course continues weekly, now emphasizing disease, disability, and rehabilitation. Students participate in Medical Interviewing and Communications Courses, involving role-play with simulated patients and personal video sessions. Clinical skills are taught and practiced in the Clinical Skills Centre and hospital wards. Two four-week Student Selected Components allow students to research topics on the molecular basis of medicine and population-based disease. Phase III (Remaining third of Year 3 and Year 4): Specialist Clinical Practice Students begin this phase with a Student Selected Component exploring ethical issues. They then observe the application of Phase II theory in clinical practice, gaining close contact with patients and their families. This phase focuses on developing diagnostic and management skills for individual patients and patient populations across all age groups and medical conditions. Phase IV (Year 5): Professional Practice This phase serves as an apprenticeship year, preparing students for competent, safe, and professional medical practice as Foundation House Officers. It includes four courses where students explore clinical areas of personal interest while practicing core medical skills under supervision. The remaining course is a project-based elective on a medical topic, often conducted overseas. Intercalated Degree At the end of Phase II, students have the option to undertake a one-year intercalated Honours Biomedical Science degree. This program includes both taught and research elements, allowing students to study a specific area of biomedical or clinical science in depth. Each student works on an individual research project, gaining skills in research methodology and critical evaluation. Medical Society (MedSoc) The Aberdeen MedSoc, the oldest student society at the university, was established to foster social connections among medical students. It currently has over 600 members and organizes annual events such as the MedSoc Ball, Doctors vs. Medics Sports Day, and a Fashion Show benefiting a local children’s charity. The committee is composed of Phase III students, with Miss Kirsten Wade serving as the current president.
